claims.text: The initial alloy is an as-cast, homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a uniform chemical distribution.
High-strain-rate or cyclic service-like loading induces local compositional segregation, nanoscale precipitation, or formation of short-range order along dislocation paths.
Cyclic mechanical loading can produce local structural evolution associated with dislocations, stacking faults, twin boundaries, and short-range order.
The loading-induced changes are concentrated in regions of high dislocation density.
Dislocations and stress concentrations under strain promote local elemental redistribution.
Mechanical activation overcomes the alloy's initial chemical homogeneity and creates segregation or precipitates.
Segregation, nanoscale precipitates, or short-range ordering inhibit dislocation mobility.
The induced microstructural features suppress crack-tip deformation and impair intrinsic toughening mechanisms.
The proposed loading-induced microstructural evolution reduces fracture toughness and shifts failure from ductile to brittle fracture.
Loaded specimens will exhibit detectable nanoscale compositional or structural modifications relative to an undeformed as-cast control.
Loaded specimens will have measurably lower fracture toughness than the as-cast control.
Loaded specimens will show cleavage or intergranular fracture rather than ductile dimpled fracture.
The undeformed as-cast baseline exhibits ductile fracture and good toughness.
Thermal exposure and impurities can drive nanoscale phase segregation and alter mechanical properties in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed effect applies under high-strain-rate or cyclic-fatigue loading at relevant operational temperatures.
The kinetics, scale, and dominant type of microstructural evolution may vary with alloy composition, loading parameters, and temperature.
A controlled comparison between service-loaded specimens and undeformed specimens can test for correlated changes in microstructure, toughness, stress-strain response, and fracture morphology.
The hypothesis is falsified if loaded specimens show no detectable segregation, ordering, or nanoprecipitates and retain toughness and fracture behavior similar to the control.
